# Exploratory Data Analysis

::: {.callout-note title="Connection with the theoretical volume"}
Probability, statistics, covariance, and multivariate representation are developed in greater depth in Chapters 2 and 3 of *Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning* [@rodriguez2026fundamentos].
:::

## Chapter objectives

By the end of this chapter, the reader will be able to load a prepared dataset, inspect its structure, compute frequencies, build exploratory graphics, compare distributions, and interpret initial patterns without confusing an educational sample with a real population.

## Why explore before modeling?

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the stage in which we learn how the variables are distributed, how categories are represented, where imbalance may exist, and which observations or patterns deserve attention before fitting a model.

EDA is not merely decorative visualization. It helps identify:

- class imbalance;
- unusual or impossible values;
- concentration by time or category;
- potentially informative predictors;
- differences between absolute frequencies and relative proportions;
- possible data-quality problems that may affect later models.

::: {.callout-warning title="Description is not causation"}
An exploratory association does not establish a causal relationship. EDA helps formulate questions and detect patterns, but causal interpretation requires a different design and stronger assumptions.
:::

# Applied Case A: ATUS

## Load packages and the prepared ATUS dataset

```{r load-atus-eda}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
source("../util_graficas.R")

atus_path <- "../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv"

if (file.exists(atus_path)) {
  atus_ml <- read_csv(atus_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  message("Prepared ATUS dataset loaded successfully.")
} else {
  atus_ml <- NULL
  warning("../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv was not found. Run Chapter 2 first.")
}
```

## Prepare variables for exploration

The source dataset keeps its original Spanish variable names because the same prepared file is shared across both language editions and the Colab notebooks. For the English graphics, we create display variables with English category labels.

```{r prepare-atus-eda}
if (!is.null(atus_ml)) {
  atus_ml <- atus_ml |>
    mutate(
      ID_HORA_NUM = as.numeric(ID_HORA),
      MES_NUM = as.numeric(MES),
      MONTH = factor(
        sprintf("%02d", MES_NUM),
        levels = sprintf("%02d", 1:12)
      ),
      accident_class = factor(
        accidente_con_victimas,
        levels = c("Con víctimas", "Solo daños"),
        labels = c("With casualties", "Property damage only")
      )
    )
}
```

## Distribution of the response variable

```{r outcome-distribution-atus, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
if (!is.null(atus_ml)) {
  class_table <- table(atus_ml$accident_class)
  round(100 * prop.table(class_table), 2)

  ggplot(atus_ml, aes(x = accident_class, fill = accident_class)) +
    geom_bar(width = 0.7) +
    escala_clases_fill() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = etiqueta_numero) +
    labs(
      title = "Distribution of accidents by casualty status",
      subtitle = "Comparison between the two modeling classes",
      x = "Class",
      y = "Number of accidents",
      fill = "Class"
    ) +
    tema_libro() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Interpretation"}
ATUS may be class-imbalanced. A majority class does not invalidate the analysis, but it means that overall accuracy alone may be misleading. Later chapters therefore use additional evaluation metrics.
:::

## Accidents by month

```{r accidents-by-month, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
if (!is.null(atus_ml)) {
  accidents_month <- atus_ml |>
    count(MONTH, name = "n") |>
    arrange(MONTH)

  ggplot(accidents_month, aes(x = MONTH, y = n)) +
    geom_col(fill = col_azul, width = 0.75) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = etiqueta_numero) +
    labs(
      title = "Number of accidents by month",
      subtitle = "Prepared ATUS dataset",
      x = "Month",
      y = "Number of accidents"
    ) +
    tema_libro()
}
```

::: {.callout-note title="What this graph can and cannot tell us"}
Monthly differences describe the records in the dataset. They do not by themselves explain why accidents increase or decrease in a particular month. Exposure, mobility, holidays, weather, reporting practices, and many other factors may be involved.
:::

## Accidents by hour of day

```{r accidents-by-hour, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
if (!is.null(atus_ml)) {
  accidents_hour <- atus_ml |>
    count(ID_HORA_NUM, name = "n") |>
    arrange(ID_HORA_NUM)

  ggplot(accidents_hour, aes(x = ID_HORA_NUM, y = n)) +
    geom_col(fill = col_turquesa, width = 0.75) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:23) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = etiqueta_numero) +
    labs(
      title = "Number of accidents by hour of day",
      x = "Hour of day",
      y = "Number of accidents"
    ) +
    tema_libro()
}
```

## Most frequent accident types

The official category labels in `TIPACCID` are retained as published in the prepared Mexican source data.

```{r most-frequent-accident-types, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.8}
if (!is.null(atus_ml)) {
  top_accident_types <- atus_ml |>
    count(TIPACCID, name = "n") |>
    slice_max(n, n = 10)

  ggplot(top_accident_types, aes(x = reorder(TIPACCID, n), y = n)) +
    geom_col(fill = col_azul, width = 0.75) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = etiqueta_numero) +
    labs(
      title = "Most frequent accident types",
      subtitle = "Official ATUS categories are preserved",
      x = "Accident type",
      y = "Number of accidents"
    ) +
    tema_libro()
}
```

## Proportion of casualty accidents by type

```{r casualty-proportion-by-type, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
if (!is.null(atus_ml)) {
  top_types <- atus_ml |>
    count(TIPACCID) |>
    slice_max(n, n = 10) |>
    pull(TIPACCID)

  atus_top_types <- atus_ml |>
    filter(TIPACCID %in% top_types)

  ggplot(atus_top_types, aes(x = TIPACCID, fill = accident_class)) +
    geom_bar(position = "fill") +
    coord_flip() +
    escala_clases_fill() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = etiqueta_porcentaje) +
    labs(
      title = "Casualty proportion by accident type",
      x = "Accident type",
      y = "Proportion",
      fill = "Class"
    ) +
    tema_libro()
}
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Interpretation"}
This graph compares **relative proportions**, not absolute counts. A rare category can show a high casualty proportion while still containing only a small number of total observations.
:::

# Applied Case B: COVID-19

## Load the same period selected in Chapter 2

To preserve reproducibility across chapters, the COVID-19 exploratory analysis uses the same comparison table and selection criterion introduced in Chapter 2 rather than simply taking the first file found in a directory.

```{r load-covid-eda}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

covid_counts <- read_csv(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados/conteo_casos_confirmados_2020_2025.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

selected_year <- covid_counts |>
  filter(
    ESTADO == "PROCESADO",
    !is.na(CASOS_CONFIRMADOS)
  ) |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = CASOS_CONFIRMADOS,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  pull(ANIO)

covid_path <- file.path(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados",
  paste0("covid19_mexico_", selected_year, "_ml_preparado.csv.gz")
)

if (!file.exists(covid_path)) {
  covid <- NULL
  warning("The prepared COVID-19 dataset selected in Chapter 2 was not found.")
} else {
  covid <- read_csv(covid_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(
      outcome = factor(
        MURIO,
        levels = c(0, 1),
        labels = c("No recorded death", "Recorded death")
      ),
      patient_type = factor(
        TIPO_PACIENTE,
        levels = c(0, 1),
        labels = c("Outpatient", "Hospitalized")
      )
    )

  message("COVID-19 dataset loaded for year: ", selected_year)
}
```

::: {.callout-note title="Source and scope"}
The prepared data are derived from historical open records published by Mexico's Ministry of Health [@salud_covid_historicos_2022]. The examples are educational analyses of administrative data and are not clinical prediction tools.
:::

## Age distribution by recorded outcome

```{r covid-age-distribution, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
#| fig-cap: "Age distribution according to the recorded administrative outcome."

if (!is.null(covid)) {
  ggplot(covid, aes(x = EDAD, fill = outcome)) +
    geom_histogram(
      bins = 35,
      position = "identity",
      alpha = 0.6
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~ outcome, ncol = 1) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c(
        "No recorded death" = col_turquesa,
        "Recorded death" = col_coral
      )
    ) +
    labs(
      x = "Age",
      y = "Frequency",
      fill = "Outcome"
    ) +
    tema_libro()
}
```

## Observed outcome by age group

```{r covid-age-groups}
if (!is.null(covid)) {
  age_summary <- covid |>
    mutate(
      age_group = cut(
        EDAD,
        breaks = c(-Inf, 19, 39, 59, 69, 79, Inf),
        labels = c("0-19", "20-39", "40-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80 or older")
      )
    ) |>
    group_by(age_group) |>
    summarise(
      records = n(),
      recorded_deaths = sum(MURIO, na.rm = TRUE),
      sample_proportion = mean(MURIO, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  age_summary
}
```

## Comorbidities and recorded outcome

```{r covid-comorbidities-outcome}
if (!is.null(covid)) {
  covid |>
    group_by(NUM_COMORBILIDADES) |>
    summarise(
      records = n(),
      sample_death_proportion = mean(MURIO, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}
```

::: {.callout-important title="Educational sample"}
If the dataset used for an exercise was stratified or balanced for teaching purposes, the proportions computed in this chapter describe **that sample**. They must not be interpreted as epidemiological rates, population mortality, or prevalence. This distinction becomes especially important when predicted probabilities are studied with logistic regression.
:::

## Questions to ask after the exploratory analysis

Before fitting a model, the reader should be able to answer questions such as:

- Is the response variable balanced or strongly imbalanced?
- Are some time periods or categories much more frequent than others?
- Are there variables with unusual concentrations or missing values?
- Does a high proportion correspond to a large number of observations or only to a small category?
- Are the patterns being described from the full source data or from an educational sample?
- Which observations suggest hypotheses worth testing in later chapters?

## Interactive laboratory: exploring distributions

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Select a numeric variable from the built-in `iris` dataset and compare its histogram, density estimate, or boxplot by species.

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 700
#| components: [viewer]

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Interactive data explorer"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput(
        "variable",
        "Variable",
        choices = names(iris)[1:4],
        selected = "Sepal.Length"
      ),
      radioButtons(
        "plot_type",
        "Plot type",
        choices = c(
          "Histogram" = "hist",
          "Boxplot by species" = "box",
          "Density" = "density"
        )
      ),
      sliderInput(
        "bins",
        "Number of histogram intervals",
        min = 5,
        max = 30,
        value = 12
      )
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("plot", height = "420px"),
      tableOutput("summary")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  values <- reactive({
    iris[[input$variable]]
  })

  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    x <- values()

    if (input$plot_type == "hist") {
      hist(
        x,
        breaks = input$bins,
        main = paste("Histogram of", input$variable),
        xlab = input$variable
      )
    } else if (input$plot_type == "box") {
      boxplot(
        x ~ iris$Species,
        xlab = "Species",
        ylab = input$variable,
        main = paste(input$variable, "by species")
      )
    } else {
      plot(
        density(x),
        lwd = 3,
        main = paste("Density of", input$variable),
        xlab = input$variable
      )
      grid()
    }
  })

  output$summary <- renderTable({
    x <- values()

    data.frame(
      N = length(x),
      Mean = round(mean(x), 3),
      Median = round(median(x), 3),
      SD = round(sd(x), 3),
      Minimum = min(x),
      Maximum = max(x)
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
### Laboratory available in the web edition
The interactive version allows the reader to select a variable and display a histogram, density curve, or species-specific boxplot together with descriptive statistics.
:::

## Chapter summary

Exploratory data analysis reveals structure, imbalance, concentrations, and relationships before models are fitted. In the ATUS route, the chapter studies frequencies and relative proportions of traffic accidents. In the COVID-19 route, it explores age, comorbidities, and an administrative outcome while maintaining a strict distinction between description of an educational sample and inference about a population.
